title: The Family Tree of Modern Languages
summary: The languages of today descend from a few ancestors - C's syntax, Simula's objects, Lisp's functions. C++ added objects to C; Python made code read like plain English; Java and C# brought virtual machines and garbage collection; JavaScript took over the web; Rust and Go rethought systems programming. Each one trades speed, safety and convenience differently.
markdown:
## Objects: Simula and Smalltalk

A new idea arrived in Norway: **Simula** (1967), by Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard, was built to simulate things like ships and queues, and introduced **classes and objects**: a bundle of data and the functions that work on it. **Smalltalk** (1972, Alan Kay and others at Xerox PARC) made objects the centre of everything, and also gave us much of the modern graphical interface.

## The family tree

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    ALGOL["ALGOL 60"] --> C["C (1972)"]
    Simula["Simula (1967)"] --> CPP
    C --> CPP["C++ (1985)"]
    CPP --> Java["Java (1995)"]
    CPP --> CS["C# (2000)"]
    Java --> CS
    C --> Go["Go (2009)"]
    CPP --> Rust["Rust (2015)"]
    ABC["ABC"] --> Py["Python (1991)"]
    Smalltalk["Smalltalk (1972)"] --> Java
    Lisp["Lisp (1958)"] --> JS["JavaScript (1995)"]
    Java -.name and syntax.-> JS
    JS --> TS["TypeScript (2012)"]
    ObjC["Objective-C (1984)"] --> Swift["Swift (2014)"]
```

| Language | Year | Made by | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C++** | 1985 | Bjarne Stroustrup, Bell Labs | C's speed with Simula's classes. Games, browsers, game engines, anything where speed matters |
| **Python** | 1991 | Guido van Rossum | Readable, short code; "batteries included" library. Science, data, AI, scripting, teaching |
| **Java** | 1995 | James Gosling, Sun | Write once, run anywhere on the JVM; garbage collection. Android apps, big business systems |
| **JavaScript** | 1995 | Brendan Eich, Netscape (in about ten days) | Make web pages interactive. Now runs everywhere, servers included |
| **C#** | 2000 | Anders Hejlsberg, Microsoft | Microsoft's Java-like language for .NET. Windows apps, the Unity game engine |
| **Go** | 2009 | Google (including Ken Thompson of Unix) | Simple, fast to compile, built for servers and concurrency |
| **TypeScript** | 2012 | Microsoft (Hejlsberg again) | JavaScript with types, to catch mistakes before running |
| **Swift** | 2014 | Apple | A safer replacement for Objective-C on Apple devices |
| **Rust** | 2015 | Mozilla (started by Graydon Hoare) | C++'s speed without its memory bugs, checked by the compiler |

## Choosing a trade-off

Languages differ mostly in what they make easy and what they make you handle yourself:

| Question | Closer to the machine | Further from it |
|---|---|---|
| Who frees memory? | You (C, C++), or the compiler's rules (Rust) | A garbage collector (Java, C#, Python, JavaScript, Go) |
| When are types checked? | Before running: **static** (C, C++, Java, C#, Rust, Go, TypeScript) | While running: **dynamic** (Python, JavaScript) |
| How is it run? | Compiled to machine code (C, C++, Rust, Go, Swift) | Bytecode and a VM, or an interpreter (Java, C#, Python, JavaScript) |
| Typical speed | Fastest | Slower, but JITs close much of the gap |
| Typical effort | More code, more control | Less code, less control |

There is no best language, only better fits. A game engine wants C++; a quick data analysis wants Python; a web page needs JavaScript; an operating system kernel wants C or, more and more, Rust.

## Paradigms

Languages also differ in **style**, called paradigms, and most modern ones mix several:

- **Procedural**: a sequence of steps and functions (C, early Python).
- **Object-oriented**: objects with data and methods (Java, C#, C++, Python).
- **Functional**: functions that take and return functions, values that do not change (Lisp, Haskell, and parts of JavaScript, Python and Rust).

## Still all the same underneath

Whatever the language, the end is the same: machine code running on a CPU, fetch, decode, execute, bits in registers and memory. A Python list, a Java object and a C array are all, in the end, bytes at addresses. The next lesson follows one line of Python all the way there.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? Which language added classes to C?
- Java
+ C++
- C#
> Bjarne Stroustrup's "C with Classes" became C++ in 1985.

? What is the main idea of Rust?
- Running programs in web browsers
+ C's speed with memory bugs caught early
- Being the easiest language for beginners
> Rust aims for the speed of C and C++, and its compiler checks who owns each piece of memory, catching memory mistakes before the program runs.

? What does "statically typed" mean?
- Variables never change
+ Types are checked before the program runs
- The language has no types
> C, Java, Rust and TypeScript check types at compile time; Python and JavaScript at run time.
```
